steps.intro: The strip across the top of every screen: ☰ menu, session name, chat/terminal switch.

steps.path: The pill in the middle of the top bar, on a phone or a window under 640 wide
steps.headline: How should the top bar show which session you are in on a phone?
steps.today: On a phone the session pill squeezes down to the first two letters of the name ("fi") next to "+10" and an arrow. On a computer the same pill shows several session names side by side.
steps.problem: You cannot read which session you are in. "+10" means nothing to a new person, and the letters are cut off mid-word.
steps.proposal: Three ways to make the current session's name readable. All keep one tap to reach your other sessions.

options.label: Full name, small count
options.summary: The pill shows only the current session's full name; a small number bubble on its arrow says how many others exist.
pros: Looks and works like the computer version, just tidier, so nothing new to learn.
Smallest change; the session list still opens from the same spot.
cons: Long names still cut off after about 18 letters.
The number bubble can be mistaken for unread messages.

options.label: Plain title, tap to switch
options.summary: The pill becomes a plain heading ("fix chat scroll ▾"), the way messaging apps title a chat. Tapping it opens the session list.
pros: Most room for the name; reads like every other phone app.
Calmer top bar with one less boxed shape.
cons: Phone and computer top bars start to look different.
Nothing hints that other sessions are running unless you tap.

options.label: Sessions in a side drawer
options.summary: The top bar shows only the name. Sessions move into a panel that slides in from the left (from ☰ or a swipe), like Gmail's folders.
pros: Room for a long, roomy list with folders and status.
Matches the phone apps most people already use.
cons: Biggest change; the ☰ menu and the session list would have to merge.
Swiping from the left edge clashes with Android's own Back swipe on many phones.

steps.path: The ☰ menu on the left and the chat/terminal button on the right
steps.headline: Where should the top bar's buttons go on a phone?
steps.today: On a phone, Settings, Projects, Pages, Session files, Browser and Games all hide behind ☰ on the left. The chat/terminal switch sits alone on the right.
steps.problem: Everything except chat is two taps away, and the terminal switch takes space from the session name even though most people never use the terminal.
steps.proposal: Three arrangements, from smallest change to biggest.

options.label: Keep, fix the details
options.summary: Same buttons in the same places; fix the hover labels that get stuck on screen after a tap (seen in the 2026-11-01 Android test).
pros: No relearning for anyone who already uses it.
Fixes the one bug people actually hit.
cons: The session name stays squeezed between two buttons.

options.label: Terminal into ☰
options.summary: "Switch to terminal" becomes a row in the ☰ menu; the top bar is only ☰ and the session name.
pros: About 40 more pixels for the session name.
Hides a developer-only control from everyday users.
cons: People who do use the terminal on a phone need an extra tap.
Getting back to chat from the terminal needs its own visible button.

options.label: Bottom tab bar
options.summary: A row of four tabs along the bottom: Chat, Projects, Pages, More — like Instagram or Spotify.
pros: Your most-used places are one thumb-tap away.
Easiest for a phone user to discover.
cons: Takes about 56 pixels of height from the chat on every screen.
Sits right below the message box and its pills, making the bottom crowded.
Largest build; desktop and phone would navigate differently.

steps.path: The blue REMOTE label beside ☰ when a phone browser is connected to your computer
steps.headline: Should the REMOTE label stay as a word in the top bar on phones?
steps.today: When you open YouCoded in a phone browser connected to your computer, a blue "REMOTE" label sits next to ☰.
steps.problem: It costs space the session name needs, and "remote" is a technical word.
steps.proposal: Three ways to keep the information with less room.

options.label: Small computer icon
options.summary: A small computer icon on the ☰ button; tapping ☰ shows "Connected to Destin's computer" at the top of the menu.
pros: Frees the space; still visible at a glance.
Plain-language explanation one tap away.
cons: An icon is easier to miss than a word.

options.label: Only in the menu
pros: Cleanest top bar.
cons: Nothing on screen tells you the phone is driving a computer.

options.label: Keep the word
pros: Unmissable.
cons: Keeps squeezing the session name.

steps.intro: What you see after tapping the session name.

steps.path: Tap the session name in the top bar
steps.headline: How should the session list open on a phone?
steps.today: It drops down from the top bar as a box that leaves a margin on both sides and ends in Resume and New session buttons.
steps.problem: The list starts at the top of the screen, the hardest place to reach with a thumb, and the box is narrower than the phone, so names and folders get cut off.
steps.proposal: Three shapes for the same list.

options.label: Slides up from the bottom
options.summary: A panel rises from the bottom, full width, with New session and Resume at the bottom edge. Swipe down or tap outside to close.
pros: Everything in thumb reach.
Full phone width, so names fit.
Familiar from Google Maps, share menus, etc.
cons: Opens far from the name you tapped at the top.
Phone and computer lists move differently.

options.label: Same dropdown, full width
pros: Least change; opens right under what you tapped.
Same as the computer.
cons: Bottom rows and the New session button are a long reach.

options.label: Its own full screen
options.summary: A whole screen titled "Sessions" with a Back arrow, like a chat list in WhatsApp.
pros: The most room, for search and filters too.
Clearest on the smallest phones.
cons: Switching feels heavier: you leave the chat to do it.
Hides the chat you were in while you choose.

steps.path: Each row of the session list
steps.headline: What should each session row show on a phone?
steps.today: Each row shows name, folder, assistant and model, status (Working/Inactive), a pin and tags, crammed into two lines; model and folder names get cut off ("w…", "Gemini 2.5 …").
steps.problem: The row tries to say six things in a phone's width, so most of them end up unreadable.

options.label: Name, folder, status
options.summary: Line 1: name and a colored status dot. Line 2: folder and tags. The assistant and model show only on the session you are in.
pros: Everything shown is readable.
Keeps what you use to pick a session: its name and where it works.
cons: You cannot see which model another session uses without switching to it.

options.label: Name and status only
pros: Simplest, one line per session, so more fit on screen.
cons: Two sessions with similar names are hard to tell apart.

options.label: Everything, three lines
pros: Nothing hidden.
cons: Rows twice as tall; about 4 fit on screen instead of 7.

steps.path: Heading of the session list on a phone
steps.headline: On a phone, the list heading says "Your sessions" instead of "Sessions in this window".
steps.changed: A phone has no windows, so the computer's wording is swapped for plain words. The 2026-11-01 Android test flagged this.
steps.notice: Same list, clearer heading. Nothing changes on a computer.

steps.page: The pills around the message box
steps.intro: The shortcut row above the message box and the row of pills below it.

steps.path: The row under the message box: model, permissions, tags, helpers, theme, version
steps.headline: How should the pills under the message box fit on a phone?
steps.today: Model, permission mode ("NORMAL"), tags, helpers running, theme name and more sit in a row that wraps onto a second line on a phone, plus a pencil to choose which ones show.
steps.problem: Two rows of small pills eat chat space, and several (theme name, version) don't matter on a phone.
steps.proposal: Three ways to bring it back to one row.

options.label: Fewer pills on phones
options.summary: Phones show only model, permissions and live activity (helpers, usage when close to a limit). The rest stay in the pencil menu, off by default on phones.
pros: One clean row; the important pills stay one tap away.
You can still turn any pill back on.
cons: Phone and computer show different pills by default, which can surprise someone using both.

options.label: One row, swipe sideways
options.summary: Keep every pill but in one row you swipe left/right, with a fade at the edge to show there is more.
pros: Nothing removed.
cons: Pills off the edge are easy to forget exist.
Sideways swiping near the message box is easy to trigger by accident.

options.label: One summary pill
options.summary: A single pill ("Sonnet · Normal ▾") opens a panel listing everything the row shows today.
pros: Calmest look; most chat space.
cons: Changing the model or mode takes an extra tap.
Live warnings (usage near a limit) are hidden unless they force their way into the pill.

steps.path: The row of shortcut chips just above the message box (Journal, Inbox, Git Status…)
steps.headline: What should happen to the shortcut chips above the message box on a phone?
steps.today: A row of chips you can tap to send a ready-made message. On a phone it runs off the right edge ("Briefi…") with nothing showing you can swipe for more.
steps.problem: It looks broken where it is cut off, and it costs a row of chat space all the time, even mid-conversation.

options.label: Fade edge; hide while typing
options.summary: Add a fade at the cut-off edge, and hide the row while the keyboard is open.
pros: Shows there is more to swipe to.
Gives the chat its space back exactly when the keyboard steals it.
cons: You cannot tap a shortcut while typing (you rarely would).

options.label: Behind a button
options.summary: The row goes away; a ⚡ button inside the message box opens the shortcuts as a list.
pros: Frees a whole row permanently.
Room for longer shortcut names.
cons: Shortcuts become less visible, so new users may never find them.
One more icon inside an already busy message box.

options.label: Just add the fade
pros: Smallest change.
cons: Still costs a row of space at all times.

steps.page: Inside the chat and other screens

steps.path: The assistant's replies in a chat
steps.headline: Should the assistant's replies use the full phone width?
steps.today: Replies sit in rounded bubbles with a margin on both sides; about a fifth of the screen width is empty margin. Step pills inside ("Ran a command · git status --…") cut off.
steps.problem: Long replies become tall, narrow columns, and step pills are too narrow to read.

options.label: Replies edge to edge
options.summary: On phones the assistant's replies drop the bubble and run nearly full width; your own messages keep their bubbles on the right. This is how the ChatGPT and Claude phone apps look.
pros: About 25% more words per line, so long answers are much shorter to scroll.
Step pills have room to read.
cons: Themes that style the reply bubble lose that look on phones.
Phone and computer chats look different.

options.label: Keep bubbles, slimmer margins
pros: Themes keep working as designed.
Some extra width.
cons: Only about 10% wider; step pills still cut off.

options.label: Leave as is
pros: No change.
cons: Problem stays.

steps.path: Pages, Projects, Settings, and any screen with a list on the left and details on the right
steps.headline: On a phone, every side-by-side screen becomes a list first, then the details on their own screen with Back.
steps.changed: Today Pages keeps the computer's two halves on a phone, leaving a thin strip saying "No page selected" (2026-11-01 Android test). Every two-part screen would follow the phone pattern.
steps.notice: Tap an item, it fills the screen; Back (or the phone's Back) returns to the list. Computers unchanged.

steps.path: Every button and control, on phones and touch-screen laptops
steps.headline: On touch screens, buttons get finger-sized and anything that appears only on hover is always shown.
steps.changed: Small icon buttons grow to at least finger size, and controls you can only reach by hovering with a mouse (Remove, Magnify, the pencil next to session names) become always visible.
steps.notice: Fewer missed taps, nothing you cannot reach. Touch screens look slightly busier.

steps.path: A computer window dragged narrower than 640 pixels
steps.headline: Should a narrow computer window get the phone layout too?
steps.today: The app already switches a few things (the ☰ menu) when any window gets narrower than 640 pixels, phone or computer.
steps.problem: If phone changes only apply to phones, a narrow computer window keeps the cramped look.

options.label: Width decides
pros: A narrow side-by-side window on your computer gets the same fixes.
One layout to keep working, so fewer bugs.
cons: Dragging a window across 640 pixels visibly reshuffles the top bar.

options.label: Only on phones
pros: Computers never change, however narrow.
cons: Narrow computer windows stay cramped.
Two sets of rules to keep in sync.

steps.path: The areas on the earlier pages
steps.headline: Which areas should be designed and drawn first?
steps.today: Card #139 lists phone polish and the 2026-11-01 Android test (card #213) covers the welcome screen and Pages. Nothing yet covers the top bar or pills as a whole.
steps.problem: Drawing everything at once makes one very long review; picking the most-felt areas gets you a phone improvement sooner.
steps.proposal: Pick any. I would start with the top bar and session list, since you see them on every screen.

options.label: Top bar
pros: Seen on every screen.
cons: Touches the computer header code too, so needs careful checks.

options.label: Session list
pros: Pairs naturally with the top bar.
cons: Swipe-up panel is new work.

options.label: Pills and shortcuts
pros: Quick wins; mostly hiding and fading.
cons: Smaller payoff alone.

options.label: Chat width and two-part screens
pros: Biggest reading improvement.
cons: Touches every theme's look; needs checking in all of them.
